7.title: Good film
7.content:
Brian De Palma is known to be a wildly inconsistent filmmaker. From the over-rated Carrie, to the under-rated Snake Eyes, the classic Untouchables and the downright hideous Mission to Mars and Scarface, he's been through just about everything. But Mission: Impossible was his first true mega-hit. Movies from TV shows are a dime a dozen these days and are rarely taken seriously, I mean look at trash like S.W.A.T. or Dukes of Hazard, but M:I is actually supposed to be a continuation of the show, rather than a spin-off.

Tom Cruise is Ethan Hunt (no, not cockney rhyming slang) an IMF agent who's entire team is killed in a phony sting operation in Prague. Accused of being a traitor he legs it before they can nab him and assembles a team of rogue operatives to find out who the REAL traitor is. Many double-crosses and double-double crosses ensue.

For those who cannot follow the plot there are some really good set-pieces with enough tension and excitement to carry the whole movie. You'll know by now the dangling scene in the top-secret room but the best scene in the movie is the high-speed train rocketing through the English countryside. While other directors might use this as a chance to show off, De Palma keeps it as realistic as possible which makes it infinitely more cooler.

Parts of the movie may seem a bit dated now and it's weird seeing Tom Cruise look like a little boy even though he was already 33. He even sounds different. And what kind of supervillian uses floppy discs? They could have tried something a bit more high-tech there.

The M:I franchise could be a heck a lot better, I suppose. The second film was terrible and the third merely average. But they're still better than the last few Bond outings, though it ain't quite up to the rugged quality of the Jason Bourne movies.

7.title: An entertaining action-thriller, though troubled by a clunky screenplay
7.content:
While I recall this being enjoyable, it's been a very long time since I last saw it. The casting is even more impressive to me now than I understood in 1996; I have memories of fun action sequences and a muddled plot. After twenty-odd years, I've been overdue to rewatch Tom Cruise's first 'Mission: Impossible' flick. Nevermind the subsequent explosion into a major franchise; how would this hold up nearly thirty years later? Truthfully, I think there are facets of this picture that haven't aged well - not by way of being problematic or offensive, but simply in terms of the construction not holding up so well. Action spy thrillers live on building excitement for the audience with both stunts and narrative intrigue, and some of what may have been impressive in the mid-90s is less so now. Don't get me wrong, I still deeply appreciate much in these two hours, and there's a lot about the story or production that's smart, admirable, or generally well done. Much more than not everyone involved did a fine job, and overall I certainly had a good time watching. Yet in retrospect the sum total is a rather mixed bag, and while the film indeed remains enjoyable, I now think it falls more into the category of "suitable, but with no big need to watch again."

Let's get the bad news out of the way first. The production values show their age, with even the fundamental image quality being kind of plain and sterile alongside facets like adequate but stale sound design. Proving that the most basic of practical effects and tangible creations will always be superior and preferable to computer-generated imagery, even the wizards at industry darlings Industrial Light & Magic give us post-production visuals that now seem thin and obvious to the point of being a little overbearing. I remember being impressed by the revamped main theme way back when, and while it is still swell in context, like other odds and ends here it doesn't boast the same vitality. More critical than some so-so contributions from behind the scenes, however, are issues of the writing. Given fresh perspective, I'm of the mind that the plot is actually, mostly, just fine. On paper there is a compelling story here, and save for a quizzical error on the part of the antagonist that is posited as a crux of the saga, it does make perfect sense to me; hats off to David Koepp and Steven Zaillian for a solid foundation. The sticking point, however, is Koepp and Robert Towne's screenplay. There are some nice, witty moments here and there, like the scene at Ethan's new safehouse after the successful operation in Langley, or the ending. There are also instances where the dialogue thinks itself to be more clever than it is, and even more to the point, too much of the dialogue and scene writing take a cohesive, coherent plot and kind of mangle it. One has to watch and listen carefully to truly take in the entirety of the tale, not because it's ingenious and convoluted - the exact opposite, in fact, for the root material is ultimately a bit light - but just because the manner in which the tale has been rendered in the script strangely chops it up. The criticism 'Mission: Impossible' earned for its writing is, sadly, completely deserved.

There is good news, however, and what it comes down to is that despite some considerable flaws, this feature remains firmly entertaining even three decades on. I don't think most of the cast is really given that much to do, or given space to meaningfully demonstrate their skills, but it's still a blast to see the likes of Vanessa Redgrave, Emmanuelle Béart, Jean Reno, Henry Czerny, and Kristin Scott Thomas sharing the screen with the more highly billed stars, and all play their parts well. Thankfully, this first installment in the franchise came before Cruise became a tad infamous for dominating productions to the detriment of the whole (e.g., 2017's superhero wannabe 'The mummy'). The stunts and practical effects are terrific, which is indeed a credit to Cruise in no small part; in fairness to ILM, I don't think the CGI is altogether terrible, just very dated. While it mostly sticks to the background Danny Elfman's score is splendid, with some themes especially sticking in my memory; I quite love Stephen H. Burum's crisp, shrewd cinematography. Though I do also take issue with what instances of soft pacing or dull, dampening the suspense, for the most part Brian De Palma's direction is capable. And I love the filming locations, Prague above all, and the costume design, hair, and makeup are excellent. At length, the movie still ably meets its goal and serves up a worthy slice of action-thriller cinema, and in its own right this is a modern classic.

It's just unfortunate that there are sufficient faults herein to weigh down the sum total. Though unseemly for modern fare, I can forgive aspects of the production that don't stand up as well any more; except in extreme circumstances, I wouldn't lambaste older flicks for such inelegance, and it's not a huge hang-up here, either. More than anything, I wish that the screenplay were far more carefully considered. Again, there's no severe trouble in the story itself, and bolstered by the action, it's communicated well enough to keep us invested; clunky dialogue and scene writing, however, really diminishes the end result. I do like this picture, and I'm glad that I took the time to rewatch after so many years; I think most folks could get something out of it. Its lasting value is less certain, however, and in 2024 'Mission: Impossible' may broadly be more notable for kicking off what is one of Paramount's premier film series. Check it out, by all means, for in my book it's still fairly worthwhile - just be aware of its shortcomings, too, and don't necessarily go out of your way for it.

7.title: Solid action movie
7.content:
What I loved about this film was the cinematography, how they used camera angles and sound to really get across the tension and twists. The close up shots were classic nighties, and it made each character have it's own significance. The use of shadowing to fully emphasize the shadiness in the world of espionage.

Tom Cruise was also great as he swaggers his spy stuff, with effortless charm but with but then an intensity and shrewdness that made him seem always two steps ahead.

Great plot, as the twists make sense, even though if it borders on being cliche.

I am also a sucker for ridiculous spy gadgets, I mean exploding bubblegum, come ooooooon. So cheesy yet so fun.

They don't overdo the spy themes and so overall this is just a very good action thriller worthy of it's cult following.

7.title: An extra long, modernized and enhanced episode
7.content:
I've never been very keen on movies that are based on old(er) TV-series, because I've never seen the point of them, except for trying to make even more money out of a good concept of course. In a way Mission Impossible isn't any different from other movies that have been based on a series, but it still is good enough to keep you entertained for a couple of hours. Not that it is all that original. Of course it has been modernized and enhanced by using the latest special effects and computer animation their budget could buy and yes it all looks very spectacular, but in fact this isn't much else but a longer version of an average episode.

Ethan Hunt, an American agent of a secret service called the IMF, is believed to be disloyal to his employer and is suspected of having killed almost his entire team of spies. He isn't the real traitor and knows that someone else in his team or in his secret service is the real bad guy. He has to find out what really happened and who is the guy they are looking for. In the meanwhile he has to stay out of the hands of some assassins who are send after him. Will he survive? Will he find out the shocking truth? It's up to you to discover...

Don't expect an excellent and mind blowing story line. If it wasn't for the, especially at that time, stunning special effects and many plot twists, this movie would have gone by unnoticed. In fact this movie is nothing more but a 110 minutes taking roller-coaster ride. It's fun to do, but not for too many times in a row. I guess the true fans of the series will be the ones who love this movie the most. Even though I called it nothing more but a longer episode, I still give it a 7/10. It's OK, without being really special

7.title: Nostalgia
7.content:
I've read reviews on here from die hard fans who knock this film. Some have even gone as far to rate it a 1? Are you kidding me? Its insanely difficult to make even an okay movie

I think nostalgia is winning the day with the old fans of the show. The show was cool but let's face it..its not all that its now cracked up to be by the fans. It hasn't aged well at all and is hokey at times. the sequels to this film are a fun watch but ultimately crappy. Ill agree with that assessment. This film is superior to the sequels, however.

I'm sorry, I disagree with the people that have a heightened sense of nostalgia regarding this material. I can understand. At least be fair, though.

Also, Tom gets a bad rap from the older gen born in the 60s. I grew up as a child in the 80s to early 90s. From my perspective he is a fine actor.. always giving it his all. I of course watched him as an impressionable child so my perspective will be different. I'm sure people are justified in their not being fond of him and even I was initially hungry to judge him down a notch when he went all nutzo in front of the nation. His ego I can imagine is quite huge considering he's been so privileged for so long. Just the same.. we don't have to be friends with him do we? I think its cool that perspectives can be so different and its very telling. I say tom is worthwhile from where I've been sittin and I refuse to pass judgments on the man. This movie is great. Id rate it a 7.8 or 7.9 easily if I could. I don't know about an 8 so ill put down a strong 7 as my rating. Maybe ill change my mind.

7.title: A Thrilling Action Spectacle That Delivers
7.content:
"Mission Impossible" kicks off the iconic spy franchise with a bang, delivering an adrenaline-fueled ride that keeps you on the edge of your seat. Directed by Brian De Palma, this action-packed thriller is a masterclass in suspense and intrigue, leaving audiences thoroughly entertained.

Tom Cruise shines as Ethan Hunt, a skilled IMF agent who finds himself framed for a heinous crime. As he races against time to clear his name, the film takes us on a rollercoaster of twists and turns, filled with daring stunts, high-tech gadgets, and surprising revelations.

The film's plot is intricately woven, keeping viewers engaged as they try to piece together the puzzle. Brian De Palma's direction is masterful, showcasing his knack for tension-building and creating intense set pieces. From the iconic dangling scene in the vault to the heart-pounding climax, the film never loses its grip on the audience.

Tom Cruise's performance as Ethan Hunt is magnetic, capturing the character's determination and resourcefulness. His commitment to performing his own stunts adds an extra layer of authenticity to the action sequences, leaving viewers in awe. The supporting cast, including Jon Voight, Ving Rhames, and Jean Reno, deliver strong performances that complement Cruise's energy.

"Mission Impossible" is a visual treat, with stunning cinematography and sleek production design. The film's stylish aesthetics enhance the thrilling atmosphere, immersing viewers in a world of espionage and danger.

The film's soundtrack, composed by Danny Elfman, perfectly complements the on-screen action, heightening the suspense and adding to the overall experience. The iconic theme has become synonymous with the franchise and remains a standout element of the film.

In conclusion, "Mission Impossible" is a must-watch for fans of action-packed thrillers. With its engaging plot, breathtaking stunts, and captivating performances, it sets the stage for the successful franchise that follows. Strap in for a wild ride filled with suspense, excitement, and one iconic spy who refuses to back down.

7.title: A True Classic
7.content: This film is very well down. It's a well done thriller with mystery and lots of twists. It messes with your mind a bit, which I do like. And overall is a great start to a massive franchise.

7.title: Only really has its momentum, so best to strap in and go with it
7.content:
It's hard to believe that Brian De Palma's Mission: Impossible is now 22 years old. What's even harder to believe is the fact that this franchise is still going, and stronger than ever, with the sixth entry into the series, Mission: Impossible: Fallout, about to be released this very week. Despite some wobbles since, the series got off to a very strong start in the hands of De Palma who, while pissing off a few hardcore fans of the original television show with some bold character decisions, delivered a thriller that really set the heart racing. It's also aged incredibly well. While the gizmos now seem somewhat dated (the McGuffin is a floppy disk), there was always an old-fashioned broodiness about the film that has given it a timeless quality. Of course, it's all just an excuse to make Tom Cruise run, and run he certainly does.

Jim Phelps (Jon Voight) and his Impossible Mission Force (IMF) are on a mission in Prague to retrieve a list of secret agents' real identities. The mission goes awry, with most of the team (which also consists of Emmanuelle Beart, Kristin Scott Thomas and Emilio Estevez) winding up dead, leaving only Ethan Hunt (Cruise) to figure out what the hell just happened. With Hunt the only survivor, IMF director Kittridge (Henry Czerny) suspects him to be the mole within the agency he has been trying to smoke out for years. Hunt flees to try and uncover the mole himself, finding a lead in the mysterious Max, a contact the mole had been communicating with using passages from the Bible. Finding himself disavowed by the government and without a team to help him, Hunt starts recruiting, finding a brand new team in fellow disavowed agents Luther Stickell (Ving Rhames) and Franz Krieger (Jean Reno). Their first mission is to break into the CIA headquarters in Langley and steal back the list, in the hope of finding the rat and proving Hunt's innocence.

There are three key set-pieces in Mission: Impossible that perhaps no other director is better suited for. De Palma is the master of long, tension-building moments of suspense, and Hunt's infiltration of the CIA is an iconic moment for good reason. He must enter into a room from above, copy a file while dangling from a wire, and exit within a set time. Any noise above a certain decibel level will trigger an alarm and cause a total lockdown, as will any additional weight on the floor. Filmed in complete silence, it's a masterfully choreographed sequence. As a trickle of sweat makes its way to the rim of Hunt's glasses, you won't exhale until it's all over. De Palma is better known for leaning of Hitchcockian influences, but his approach here is more Jules Dassin. There are other exciting moments too, and thank God, as the plot is about as baffling as its lead stars affiliation with Scientology. The thrills also distract from some pacing issues, which normally arise when Hunt is left to mope around in a hotel room, and some revelations you can see coming from a mile off (the shifty, knife-wielding Frenchman is a baddie, really?). Mission: Impossible really only has its momentum, so it's best just to strap in and go with it.

7.title: Clone faces and the End of the Movie
7.content: It's a good movie, interesting, especially in terms of action. There are mistakes and there is a serious one that is decisive: If it is possible to perfectly clone someone's face, then what is the value of a film to prove that someone is alive? And there could be a helper at the end of the movie.

7.title: S10 Reviews: Mission: Impossible (1996)
7.content:
Impossible Missions Force operative Ethan Hunt (Tom Cruise) is on the run when a mission goes horribly wrong and his fellow teammates are killed. The mission to protect the list and identities of all the undercover operatives failed and Hunt is set up to take the blame. Hunt must get to the bottom of the conspiracy, find the list and save his name.

The small screen classic finally gets a big screen treatment. Brian DePalma directs a reasonably taunt action thriller that diverges a bit for the original series but since this is a star vehicle for Cruise that is to be expected. The acting seems a bit stiff throughout 'Mission' but it moves at a solid pace and has a few cool action setpieces. A few cheesy digital effects aside 'Mission: Impossible' is a solid action franchise starter.

7.title: 60s Series Reborn On the Screen
7.content: Tom Cruise stars in the rebirth of a 60s TV staple as he brings "Mission: Impossible" to the big screen. The popular TV show is infused with new blood as we follow the trail of Impossible Mission Force agent Ethan Hunt (Cruise) as he is framed for the death of his team while on a mission. He looks up disavowed members of the force to form a new team to help him clear his name. Standout turns by Jean Reno and Ving Rhames as new members of his team, they look to find the "mole" who has betrayed the Force as well try to find out who is looking to steal the list of identities of all the IMF agents. Brian DePalma directed this initial entry of the new film franchise, which was controversial upon its release due to its treatment of one of the original characters, Jim Phelps, played by Jon Voight. Although fans of the original TV series were up in arms, the film was still enjoyable, with enough intrigue and twists to keep viewers interested.

7.title: Try any sleight of hand with my money and I'll cut your throat.
7.content:
This film is full of stars, including two of my favorites, Jean Reno and Kristin Scott Thomas.

The plot is a little difficult to follow, with all the double-dealing, but not to worry. It has all the usual spy stuff: spyglasses, hidden microphones, laptops, elaborate disguises, exploding cars, knifings, shootings, bodies toppling into a river, etc

Basically, a mole has broken into the group's inner circle; the mission was an attempt to flush him out. But instead of exposing the real culprit, it throws suspicion on team member Ethan Hunt (Tom Cruise), who is forced to go underground to prove his innocence.

We've seen some of this in Jules Dassin films, but not even Bond has a chase scene like the one here.

The bottom line on a film like this is, Tom Cruise looks cool and holds our attention while doing neat things that we don't quite understand

7.title: A thrilling classic!
7.content:
Mission Impossible is an exciting spy movie that has become a classic. Some might find it a bit confusing to follow the story, but if you manage, the story is very good. There are many good twists and turns that you don't see coming. The acting is great with many famous actors.

However, this movie has some really stupid scenes.

At the beginning of the film in the first mission, Sarah sees Golitsyn being murdered near a gate. This highly-trained Sarah runs up to the gate without taking out any weapon and lets herself be stabbed to death. How stupid can you be? Also, the way Jim fakes his death is just weird and not well thought out. The other agents can see what Jim sees through his glasses. So the gun is supposed to be aimed straight at Jim's head when he gets shot. When we find out later that Jim fakes his death, this angle is apparently filmed from another camera next to Jim and Jim still has his glasses on, which doesn't make any sense. Even getting your hand and arm in that angle, pointed at your face with a gun with a silencer, is kind of impossible. Try it yourself and imagine that you are holding a gun that you are about to fire.

The most exciting part in the whole movie is when they are going to break into the vault, but it is also the most poorly thought out, which bothered me a bit. Since it is so important not to sweat and drip sweat on the pressure plates, it would have been good to have a headband or a shroud and a thin shirt with long sleeves instead of a t-shirt that can keep the sweat from dropping on the floor. How could they not think of that? And how did he catch that drop of sweat? Look at the position he is in, and then the frame with the hand catching that drop. Why does Ethan bring two disks with him during this mission if he's only going to use one? And why is Krieger so slow to pull Ethan back up? Why does Krieger even have his knife out? How come this vault doesn't have a single camera?

The scene at the end with the helicopter inside the tunnel was also a bit ridiculous. When Ethan puts the exploding gum on the helicopter which causes the helicopter to blow up and with the help of the shock wave Ethan gets back on the train. I mean, come one.

Apart from these things, it is a very good and exciting spy movie.

7.title: Good and bad, thrilling and frustrating.
7.content:
Mild spoilers ahoy. Can one really spoil a 19 year old film though?

I very much enjoyed this film when seeing it on its initial release in 1996, at the fabulous Empire, Leicester Square, London. Whilst never a die-hard fan of the TV series, I had been entertained and absorbed by it, and I liked that they attempted to introduce many elements of that series into the big-screen incarnation whilst broadening it out with big action sequences (notably the Channel Tunnel finale) to cater for the 90s Blockbuster audience. And this is why the film both thrills and annoys me.

The throwbacks are all nice (the masks, the intricate con-job set- ups etc), but ultimately undone by the decision to make an action- leaning set-piece laden film. They were largely jettisoned as the franchise progressed, which is fine, but I felt short-changed here. This may be petty, but having Jim Phelps (for those that don't know, the protagonist and hero of the series from its second series onward) turn out to be the villain was just plainly unforgivable. Imagine if the "Star Trek" reboot had cast James T Kirk as the antagonist. That left a real sour taste in the mouth.

I'm surprised that the screenplay was handed in by writers as esteemed as David Koepp and Robert Towne, because much of the early dialogue, notably in the session where the team are briefed, seems forced and unrealistic - Hollywood quippy rather than natural. It's not helped that Tom Cruise's performance oscillates wildly between stern, serious, and meaning business, and toothy grin, over keen to quip and be liked. Maybe it was intended for the character, but it's at odds with how I felt it should be played, and different from the later portrayals of operative Hunt. I like Cruise in the latter films but he's too "Jerry Maguire" here for me. I did love his "disc disappearing" trick in Liverpool St though, and the rest of the cast were all solid. I'm glad Ving Rhames (as Luther) has become a mainstay of the franchise, Henry Czerny fits the mould of every disgruntled MI team boss throughout the series to a tee, Emmanuelle Beart is HOT, Reno is... well, he's Jean Reno, only with more attitude. Kristin Scott Thomas adds a welcome touch of class, and the Lithuanian lady playing Hannah is also one not to KooBoaCN. And of course there's the sublime Vanessa Redgrave... very watchable all round.

The plot is not difficult to follow, despite common perception. It's just, frankly, a little silly. The idea that all this confidential information about non-confirmed agents would be stored in one place (even in the most secure room in the world, but with lousy server security) just doesn't ring true. And, incidentally, if it's the most secure room in the world, have they not thought about putting in a simple CCTV camera as well? But that's by the by. DePalma is an infamous admirer of Hitchcock, so I'm not surprised he's happy to hoist such a heinous MacGuffin on which to hang his outlandish, stylized, and highly engrossing set-pieces without too much concern for credibility. But those set pieces are impressive. The Prague setup, the raid at Max's, Langley (despite being so goofy), the train (London Terminus on the TGV - bless!), are all expertly staged and enticing scenes. There's just that niggling sense of "this could have been more" haunting the picture.

M:I 2 I'll give a pass to, M:I 3 I think hit the mark completely and utterly, and is still my favourite of the bunch. GP is fun too, and I look forward to RN next week. This first one, I keep thinking about though, because it's not bad, by any stretch of the imagination, it's just not as good as it could have been. This review will self destruct in...

7.title: This is where it all started!
7.content:
This is where the legacy of Ethan Hunt as well as the franchise in itself, had originated. This movie shaped the franchise, which we all had come to love and appreciate; this is where it all began and what an introduction it was!

One thing that I have always enjoyed about these Mission Impossible movies is that they take their impossible missions (no pun intended) seriously.

They are not just there to act as fillers or to be less important junctures to move the story forward; they are there to function as critical plot points, ultimately culminating in an action-heavy ride filled with tension and suspense!

And they maintained their style in all the entries, and that is one impressive feat, to be honest.

7.title: Light the Match
7.content: Tom Cruise is Ethan Hunt a member of Ifm, who's team is sent after a rogue agent from stealing A CIA NOC list of Agent identities. However, the mission goes sided ways and everybody except Ethan is killed. The IFM director then reveals that the mission was set up, to weed out a mole and suspects Ethan of being the mole and working for an arms dealer. Now Ethan has to seek out the arms dealer and find out who the Mole, is while being pursued by the CIA. With a spanning over 6- movies the first mission impossible remains one of those staples in the spy-espionage genre. Without a doubt, Tom cruise's most iconic role. The first mission impossible is a throwback to classic spy films focusing more on espionage, and not relying highly on the action. While there's action it doesn't come off as fast-paced and over the top as some of the later films. It's more reminiscent of the older James bond film kinda incorporates some of that 60s feel that 007 or even the original shows. How many times has that vault scene with the ropes been parodied by other spy products? The cast gives a good likable performance of course Tom Cruise is great. Jon Voight and Ving Rhames. Wish there was some more of Jean Reno, but still, the cast is overall good.

7.title: More Spy Than Action
7.content:
The first in a 26 year old franchise that has become a staple in the action genre and well known for its crazy stunts performed by Mr. Cruise.

This one is probably most known for its iconic suspended above the floor scene. It's a great scene, no doubt. But this movie definitely has a lot less action than the sequels. It's more about the spy game and solving the puzzle, that always left me slightly confused in different parts when I was younger. That very well may have been me and my 10 year old brain when it came out, but I still don't think the plot is conveyed all that well and can still be a little tricky to keep up.

The camera work and overall filming technique is dated to. A lot of still work.

7.title: A tense and tight movie adaptation
7.content:
This review contains spoilers.

Mission: Impossible is a spy action movie starring Tom Cruise as Ethan Hunt. Ethan Hunt is a part of the Impossible Missions Force which specializes in impossible missions. Ethan Hunt is framed for a mission gone wrong that causes his IMF team to be killed with Ethan Hunt as the sole survivor. Ethan seeks out the actual mole and must stay one step ahead of the authorities seeking his arrest.

Mission: Impossible is a fun movie. There are loads of action scenes that are thrilling to watch. These action scenes are the main appeal of this movie. Each action set piece is well set-up by the rest of the movie and that leads to good pacing on the director's part. It does get tiring seeing the action at times, but Tom Cruise does a good job as Ethan Hunt. He is able to convey the sheer desperation of the mission and how it close it is to failure.

The parts of the movie that are not great is when the movie slows down to develop its characters. Ethan Hunt is a two-dimensional character. He is simply an action hero in this movie. His only difference is that he does not use firearms. The movie does a good job with handling this gimmick and it was never forced onto the viewer.

I recommend Mission: Impossible. The later movies feel different compared to the original, however the original still has that charm that started the entire franchise. That charm is worth visiting here.

Grade: B.

7.title: A nice movie
7.content: Mission Impossible is a good entertaining movie. The +points of the movie are 1. Tom cruise: Tom cruise performance is awesome. 2. Stunts: Stunts are really very good. especially the one while copying the file from computer. Even though the story is ordinary one, presentation is good. Its just like Bond movies. But U cant find Mr. Cruise's wonderful performance there. Its Bond movie-Bond+Tom Cruise. But climax is not well framed. Looks comical where agent Hunk fighting on the top of super fast train and Helicopter following. Climax could have been formed better. Overall its good and entertaining. Thanks Mr. Cruise for wonderful performance.

7.title: Keep it simple please
7.content: Ludicrous and convoluted plotting almost ruins the fun in the original 1996 blockbuster. The audience just wants to see awesome action, but we are saddled with incoherent gibberish and plot twists that bewilder and confuse. Cruise is always good, and the set pieces are sensational, particular the CIA break in. De Palma tries very hard to let us know how intelligent the film is, but we would just like to see some impossible missions please. 7/10.

7.title: A good but ultimately unspecial film
7.content: This film is good if you want to see how the franchise got started, but it doesn't hold up the best on its own. I'm sure someone who grew up with this movie would absolutely adore it, but as someone with no nostalgic connection to the franchise, I think this film is the most standard of its ilk. It isn't even clear in the first 30 minutes who the main character is. It's still a well paced, thrilling, and very good film, but it isn't quite what I love about Mission Impossible, it suffers in retrospect thanks to the incredible films that came afterward. Ultimately the most normal film in the franchise, and in a lot of ways not all that memorable.

7.title: Nifty Gadgets Galore
7.content:
Celebrated actor Tom Cruise had collaborated with his agent Paula Wagner for eleven years. Then, in 1992, they decided to expand that cooperation. Together they formed the independent movie company "Cruise/Wagner Productions". The aim was to give Tom Cruise greater creative freedom, as well as to offer him full control of his own films. A dream the performer had nurtured for a long time.

After years of careful research, Tom Cruise and Paula Wagner found a perfect franchise vehicle in the form of the old TV show "Mission: Impossible". Paramount Pictures had already tried to turn the series into a movie, so when Cruise showed interest in the project they quickly green-lighted it. Glitzy old veteran Brian De Palma was hired to take care of the direction, not least for his cunning ability to keep a huge cinema audience on the edge of their seats.

In the film, a secret agent (played by Tom Cruise) is faced with a diabolical choice. Either he uncovers the mole that killed several members of his team, or the CIA will blame him for the murders.

To keep the budget down, Cruise agreed to lower his usual $20 million fee. Instead, he wanted a higher percentage of the box office - which Paramount had no problem with. However, their representatives insisted on moving the film's opening mission from Austria to the Czech Republic. Smart, since that country had invested heavily in a low-cost, state-of-the-art infrastructure since the fall of Communism.

In the summer of 1996 Paramount rolled out "Mission: Impossible" on over 3,000 screens across the country. It was the widest opening in cinema history, and the film remained in theaters until Christmas that year. Thus, Tom Cruise's gambit to work for scale had worked out great. By taking the money off the back end, the actor more than doubled his usual payday. Mission: Accomplished.

7.title: Servicable and fun enough
7.content:
This is the start of the iconic franchise that in a way can be said to have kickstarted Tom Cruise's career as not just a dramatic actor, but an action star as well -and for that it of course deserves some recognition.

It is also a film by the legendary auteur Brian De Palma (which is a bit of an unexpected choice given his typical kind of film), which in itself makes it worthwhile.

The film in itself, though, is okay and not much more. It is suspenseful enough, has some interesting characters and some cool action setpieces, but is all around pretty brainless and shallow.

It doesn't set out to do that much more than it achieves, and is a fun time for sure. It doesn't delve too much into the over-the-top as its sequels and is more of a grounded heist/spy thriller.

I would recommend it in terms of following the series, as well as adapting the iconic TV show in a pretty decent fashion. I would not call it great, though.

7.title: A nice action movie
7.content: I expected a better movie because I've saw very much commercial on it. They make us think it will gonna be such a great movie with such big actors and actress but it wasn't. It didn't have so many big stars as they said. The script is not so good as I expected. It has a some action and suspense and a pretty good direction so I guess this make it a nice action movie.

7.title: Took me a few watches, but I figured it out
7.content:
Three, actually. It's because, in regular movies, someone explains the plot outright, so the audience doesn't have to think about it. You really had to pay attention to the details to figure it out. Let's see how accurate I am.

Voight was a mole working for the CIA and was trying to steal a special list of secret operatives to sell to the enemy. To cover his tracks, he killed everyone on his team and made it look like he died with them. Cruise was taking the fall, but was determined to prove his innocence. Keeping tabs on Cruise was Voight's wife, Claire, who he happened to fall for (even though he had figured Voight wasn't dead).

So, Cruise wins the trust of a criminal ready to pay top dollar for the list and gets a new team to steal the other half of the list. He and the criminal meet on the train to exchange the list and the money, but Voight wants the money. And I'm sure you can lay everything over from there on.

It was a good movie with good actors, and nice story, and excellent action sequences. It's worth a look, and even a second look, for anyone who hasn't seen it and those who have. Very well directed.

7.title: Mission: Impossible
7.content: I'm not the biggest fan of the diminutive Mr Cruise - but I have to hand it to him here. Brian de Palma has created an end-to-end action adventure and he is superb in it. He brings oodles of charisma to the screen as he ("Ethan Hunt") has to recover from a disastrous mission and build a team to discover not only who betrayed them, but to obtain a top secret list of American overseas operatives (i.e. Spies) before it falls into enemy hands spelling doom for all concerned. What ensues is a fast-paced, well constructed movie that moves along cohesively with plenty going on - loads of tension, suspicion, nobody knowing whom to trust coupled with plenty of exciting stunts and a classy performance from Vanessa Redgrave bringing some gravitas to the proceedings as the stylish, but ruthless, "Max". Sure, it relies on tech and CGI a lot of the time, but the ensemble - Ving Rhames, Emmanuelle Béart and Jon Voight all deliver well into a plot that keeps us guessing until well into the denouement. Even Henry Czerny - not noted for the flexibility of his performances - turns in a decent effort and the ending might make you think twice before using the Chunnel! If you're looking for a good, high-octane piece of cinema; then this is certainly up there - on a big screen, if you can.

7.title: Mission Impossible
7.content:
That was a lot more fun than I expected, I think where I really began to fully get into the movie was when it was stated that the entire opening mission was a Mole Hunt. With Ethan Hunt obviously being the one to make it out I was buckled in to see him go at crazy lengths to clear his name.

The missions displayed here are so exciting to watch, nail biting at times, the near drop of sweat had me sweating, I think seeing these intricate sequences are where the movie is at its strongest.

Now to complain about something, because this movie isn't perfect, everything felt, believable I would say, so it kinda did go crazy once I saw the helicopter go down the tunnel with the train, it pulled me out completely but it wasn't enough to ruin the movie.

7.title: Mission (more or less) accomplished
7.content:
Plot; Agent Ethan Hunt is framed and must fight to both clear his name and discover the actual culprit before they can sell a list containing sensitive information.

The M:I franchise is an odd one. W/gaps of 4, 6, 5 and 4 years, it lacked any kind of set release schedule typically associated w/blockbuster franchises. And bouncing between wildly different directors, it also struggled to find a consistent tone. But for the most part they entertained and found enough success to warrant another. When director Christopher McQuarrie came on board for the series' fifth entry, the franchise once again bucked franchise convention by hitting its stride. Today, 6 films and 23 years later, the Mission: Impossible film series is more popular than ever. Having enjoyed the most recent entry, Fallout, this past Summer, I've had an itch to go back and revisit the original as a sort of compare and contrast. And contrast they do. Wildly so. I wasn't surprised by this, but that contrast wasn't exactly the type of contrast I was expecting.

M:I isn't really an action movie. At least not in the conventional sense, and certainly not in the mold of Fallout. Aside from its explosive finale, there's nothing here that I'd call an action scene. At least not in the "Bang! Bang! Zoom! Zoom!" sense. It's more of a thriller than an action movie. And like many such films from its era, it carries a whiff of Cold War zeitgeist even as it acknowledges its end. But other than that and its amusingly outdated tech, it's not as "90s" as I thought. I was expecting it to be more 90s than Bill Clinton watching Friends and drinking a Crystal Pepsi while wearing a Lollapalooza t-shirt at Beavis and Butthead's house, but it's actually got a more timeless feel.

Just as the series struggled to find a tone and style, so too has Cruise (and the writers) failed to give Ethan Hunt a definable personality or set of characteristics (beyond, perhaps, a dogged determination). Bond's personality has varied wildly over the years depending on the era and the actor, but he's had a basic set of traits and tropes to help ground him. Hunt has none of those things. Even as the last two films began to give some shape to the series, I can't give you even a thumbnail of who Ethan Hunt is. That's not to say Cruise is bad. In fact, he's quite good. Whatever limitations and range Cruise may have, he has undeniable star power, and it's an asset here. He's surrounded by a uniformly strong cast, w/Jon Voigt (though sadly not his car *90s reference*), Vanessa Redgrave, Jean Reno, Henry Czerny and series regular Ving Rhames doing top work. Redgrave and Czerny in particular are fun to watch, and I wish they'd been brought back in future entries.

In juxtaposition to Fallout, this first M:I movie is a tad slow, even though it clocks in at under 2 hours to Fallout's near 2 and a half hour runtime, but taken on its own merits it's a well made popcorn thriller w/just enough twists and turns to satisfy.

7.title: Just the beginning
7.content:
Having seen this multiple times, the twists are known. But the movie surprisingly holds up minus a few technology things. Cruise is still a baby in this movie and not the Ethan Hunt we get to know.

The turns and twists in the movie are good but often underdeveloped or unexplained. They need to spend about 90 more seconds to explain a few things. Wish some of the characters were either more developed or out of the film. Some unnecessary items make the film drag a bit. But nothing unwieldy

Overall, enjoyed the movie and what ends up being an introduction to an ongoing franchise that wows at every stop.

7.title: Ethan Hunt's labyrinthine mission: A stylish, action-packed ride!
7.content:
In 1996, Tom Cruise cemented his status as a bona fide action star with the release of "Mission: Impossible," a slick and stylish spy thriller that breathed new life into the classic TV series. Directed by Brian De Palma, this adrenaline-fueled ride takes viewers on a globetrotting adventure filled with jaw-dropping stunts, intricate plot twists, and a healthy dose of suspense.

Cruise stars as Ethan Hunt, a highly skilled agent of the Impossible Missions Force (IMF), who finds himself embroiled in a web of deception and betrayal. When his team is brutally eliminated during a mission gone awry, Hunt becomes the prime suspect and is forced to go rogue to clear his name and uncover the real mole within the IMF ranks.

De Palma's masterful direction shines through in the film's set pieces, which are nothing short of breathtaking. From the daring break-in at the CIA headquarters to the heart-stopping train heist sequence, each action sequence is meticulously choreographed and executed with precision, keeping viewers on the edge of their seats.

At the center of it all is Tom Cruise, who delivers a commanding performance as the resourceful and determined Ethan Hunt. Cruise's charisma and commitment to performing his own stunts add an extra layer of authenticity to the film, making it all the more thrilling to watch. His chemistry with co-stars Jon Voight and Emmanuelle Béart also adds depth to the character dynamics.

While the action sequences are undoubtedly the film's highlight, "Mission: Impossible" also boasts a cleverly crafted plot that keeps audiences guessing until the very end. The twists and turns are expertly woven into the narrative, ensuring that the suspense remains high throughout the film's runtime.

"Mission: Impossible" is a solid entry in the action genre, delivering on its promise of high-stakes thrills and edge-of-your-seat excitement. While it may not reinvent the spy movie formula, it executes it with style and flair, thanks to De Palma's skilled direction and Cruise's magnetic screen presence. If you're a fan of action-packed blockbusters, this mission is definitely worth accepting.

7.title: Confusing, over-the-top, but fun and smart
7.content: *WARNING MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS* Now that I've reviewed Mission: Impossible III, which I just watched, I decided to go back and review the first two MI movies, and give you my thoughts. I understand how someone would like this movie more than I do, and I can see myself liking it more on a future viewing, but as it stands now, I just think this movie is okay. I think Tom Cruise does a pretty good job as Ethan Hunt, but, and you won't hear me say this often, I thought the movie was shot poorly. The way it was shot, and just the general look of the movie made it look like it was made in 1960. Maybe that's what they were going for, but it kind of threw me. Another thing that threw me, and I get that this was intentional, was that there was almost no fighting. There are suspenseful scenes, which I will get to in just a minute, but there aren't any shootouts, and there is only one brief fistfight and a chase scene, that's it. I like that they tried to make a different spy-thriller type movie, but they could've included a bit more action, though I do think this was an interesting idea. I'm not saying it was necessarily bad, I'm just saying I expected something... different. Despite my complaints against this movie, I can't deny that I had an absolute blast watching it. The break-in at the HQ building was very tense, but also very funny. The two don't sound like they'd work well together, but I think they mixed the two styles very nicely in this scene. The investigation was rather confusing to me, maybe I just missed some crucial plot point, but I was lost for a large chunk of this movie, which might have hurt my opinion a bit. This movie also doesn't really have a villain, exactly. It's more about Ethan on the run, and trying to figure out what's going on, but the villain, Job, is in the movie... maybe ten minutes, and it's not like he's even an opposing force when he's not on screen, there's just... no villain. The fight on the train though, that was an excellent scene. Action- packed, suspenseful, and very entertaining. Unlike 2 and 3, this movie is certainly not playing it with a straight face, this is obviously going for a humorous tone, and I think they pulled it off well. In the end Mission: Impossible was a fun movie, despite my problems with it, it had good characters, some good tension, and a smart, if confusing story.

7.title: Decent spy action movie
7.content:
After a CIA operation goes wrong, Ethan Hunt has to find out who betrayed them. Tom Cruise stars with an all star cast.

The movie that started the great series but they get better. An interesting plot with a couple twists and some very memorable moments.

7.title: Red light, green light !!
7.content:
A spy movie with realistic action scenes and good cinematography. However, the plot is quite difficult to follow, and you need to pay full attention. The dialogue is also challenging to keep up with. The script is not well written, some scenes are confusing, and there are noticeable goofs. The depiction of the internet is outdated and often illogical.

Ving Rhames is a good cast as Luther. The movie has some iconic scenes, the Langley heist is the standout, and the climactic train sequence is also very thrilling.

Overall, a Brian De Palma film, not for the fans of the original series because the teamwork dynamic has been replaced by a one-man show focused on Tom Cruise.

7.title: Time Has Not Been Kind
7.content:
So in all this time it seems I've never actually reviewed the first Mission: Impossible. I've reviewed literally every other but this one, which means it must've been nearly ten years since I last watched it. In truth it's because it scratches a completely different itch than the other five movies, an itch that I end up scratching with other movies instead. When I want to watch a Mission: Impossible movie, I want to see Tom Cruise clinging on to planes, almost dying, or getting into knife fights on a beach while a dove flies by in the foreground. The first film is not that. The movie series that Tom Cruise has personally shepherded over twenty years into one of the most successful action franchises all started with a confusing, suspense-ridden spy affair of intrigue and betrayal.

Mission: Impossible, like all the others, predominantly follows Ethan Hunt, here a young IMF agent and merely one member of a team of spies. Hunt isn't even the boss here, he's just the muscle. That is until things go wrong in Prague, and he finds himself under suspicion of stealing a disk full of names of operatives out in the field. It's on him to prove his innocence, work out who set it all up, and find the buyer for the list.

What actually surprised me the most when rewatching today was how remarkably simple the movie's structure is. It's three setpieces and some connective tissue between them. That's all. We have the opening mission in Prague, the betrayal, and Hunt put under suspicion, then we have the iconic heist in the CIA building, and then the movie closes with the climax on the train. Truth be told, when boiled down to their absolute basics, this is how a lot of movies are, but I haven't noticed it nearly as obviously as in this movie. Everything between these moments is just filler and exposition, which it was. The movie had already started building the sets before the script was even finished. The script had to be written around these three big moments, and it really shows. As a result the film is often criticised for being confusing, and I admit I always used to find it confusing as well. Except today when it all clicked perfectly and I could follow along every plot point, even though I had forgotten almost every little connective detail and crucial plot point.

So SPOILER paragraph to explain what happens for anyone who still finds themselves confused by this movie; Jim Phelps is the mole who steals the list to sell to Max. Kittridge suspects there of being a mole and sets up a mole hunt. This is the opening sequence in Prague. Phelps fakes his death, and either he or Claire blows up the car with Hannah in, while Krieger (Claire's man for the heist) kills Sarah in the alleyway. Hunt realises it was Phelps when he finds the bible from a Chicago hotel, something Phelps mentions briefly at the beginning, which was the source of the code/password to contact Max. This meant Phelps was Job, and everything else was just logical deduction. Claire is also one of the survivors, and Hunt's infatuation with her is what blinds him to her betrayal, and creates that point of uncertainty over who killed Hannah (let's be honest, it was Claire; why else would she leave the car?)

Unfortunately I can't say this movie has aged particularly well. The level of technology here is laughable when viewed today. Hunt literally types "Internet Access" into his computer, and then uses the search bar to give the computer commands. Our level of computing was certainly somewhat archaic back in the mid-90s, but even that is ridiculous. Furthermore a lot of the futuristic, out-there gadgets are not only perfectly plausible today, but by now a lot of it is old news as well. Watches that show photos/video? Wireless internet connection that gets lost in a tunnel? Glasses with tiny little cameras? But what ages this movie for me more than anything else is Danny Elfman's quintessentially 90s score. It's entirely orchestral and jam-packed full of as many themes and cues as humanly possible. A single piece barely sounds coherent, and more like a montage of different motifs that constantly chop and change into something else. If you've ever paid attention to movie scores from the 90s, you know exactly what this sound is, and Danny Elfman is the undisputed master of it, but oh god does it date the movie pretty badly.

Mission: Impossible is often hailed as the best of the series, if only by virtue of being the original (despite many die-hard fans of the 60s TV show shunning it at the time for not being faithful enough), but honestly it's probably my least favourite. Yeah, the CIA heist is iconic for a reason. Ethan Hunt suspended from the ceiling is one of the most tense scenes ever put to film. But everything else is just okay. Don't get me wrong, it is enjoyable, and I enjoyed it more today than I probably ever have done before, but when compared to the other movies, especially the brilliant McQuarrie entries, this film is just dull. It's convoluted and yet simplistic at the same time, and its most exciting moments fall flat just because their ridiculousness in an otherwise grounded and restrained movie just feel out of place (at least M:I2 is cheesy and over-the-top throughout). I give the original 1996 Mission: Impossible a respectful but unfortunately overshadowed by its successors 7/10.
